The rollout is two weeks behind schedule. I am telling you now, not at the end.
Good. What is holding it?
We are waiting for one stakeholder. Risk reviews every policy change, and they are reviewing three at the same time this month.
And the pilot? Is that stopped too?
No. The pilot is running, and we are monitoring it every morning. The numbers look normal so far.
So what do you need from me?

Quick update on the three things. First, the pilot. It is on track. We are monitoring it every morning, and this week we are adding two thousand more customers, so by Friday it covers about a third of the base. Second, the pricing rollout. It is behind schedule, and the reason is simple. We are waiting for one stakeholder. Risk reviews every policy change, and right now they are reviewing three of ours at the same time. Third, the old project. It is paused, and I am not restarting it this quarter. I know that is not popular. What I need from this call is one decision, not more people. Tell me whether risk looks at ours first or not, and I will plan around the answer.

Almost everybody puts the bad news at the end. They open with the three things that went well, they build up, and then at minute eleven they say the thing that actually matters. By then the other person has stopped listening properly, and worse, they now think you were hiding it. So put it in the first sentence, and put three things in that sentence: what the problem is, how big it is, and the fact that you are already handling it. The rollout is two weeks late, we are waiting on risk, and I am not stopping the pilot while we wait. That is one breath and the whole picture. And here is what you never do in that first sentence. Do not apologise. An apology moves the conversation to your feelings, and nobody in that meeting came to talk about your feelings. Say sorry later, if it is still true.

Before a bank changes a rule for everybody, it changes it for a few. A small group gets the new rule, a second group keeps the old one, and the two are compared. That part is not new. It is what every website does with a button. Credit is harder, and the reason is time. When you change the colour of a button you know within a day whether people click it. When you change who gets a loan, the result takes months to appear, because the customer has to miss a payment before anybody knows anything, and by then the money is already out of the door. So the teams are watching earlier signals instead. They are not waiting for the final number. They are looking at the first missed payment, at how fast the limit is used, at who calls the bank in the first week. None of those tell you the answer on its own, but together they tell you when to stop.
